share_verdict: Rasam was pepper. The tomato and the chilli are both guests.

source.text: Pre-colonial South Indian household practice, as documented in regional culinary history

ingredients.name: black pepper
ingredients.function: the heat and the point of the dish

ingredients.name: long pepper
ingredients.function: the other pepper — almost entirely gone from Indian kitchens today

ingredients.name: tamarind
ingredients.function: the sour. There is no tomato in this dish

ingredients.name: freshly crushed spices
ingredients.function: ground for the pot, not bought as a blend

method_reconstructed: Crush the peppers and spices fresh, on stone.
Temper in sesame oil or ghee and simmer.
contested_points: Long pepper (pippalī) is the ingredient most completely lost from this dish; it is not simply less common but effectively absent from everyday cooking.
The dish survives under several regional names — saar, saaru, chaaru, pulusu — which are not all the same preparation.

changed.from: black pepper and long pepper as the heat
changed.to: black pepper plus red chilli, with long pepper rarely used at all
changed.driver: chilli arrived with Portuguese trade, grew easily and cost less than pepper
the tomato is a Columbian-exchange arrival and became a cheap, year-round souring and bulking agent

changed.from: spices crushed fresh on stone for each pot
changed.driver: commercial spice blending made a consistent, shelf-stable powder cheaper than grinding

ingredients: 1 tbsp black peppercorns and 1 tsp long pepper (pippali), crushed just before cooking
A lime-sized ball of tamarind, soaked
steps: Crush the peppercorns and long pepper coarsely. Doing this fresh is most of the difference.
Extract the tamarind in warm water and strain.
Temper cumin and curry leaf in sesame oil, pour in the tamarind water, and simmer until the raw edge goes.
Add the crushed pepper at the end so it stays aromatic.
Sharper and more resinous than a tomato rasam, and the heat sits at the back of the throat instead of the front of the tongue.
